tara.question:
The new bypass was built to reduce traffic in the town centre. Since it opened, congestion in the centre has indeed fallen. However, traffic on the residential roads leading to the bypass has increased sharply, and accidents there have risen. The bypass has simply moved the problem rather than solving it.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

options.text: The bypass was built to reduce town-centre traffic.
Congestion in the town centre has fallen.
The bypass has moved the traffic problem rather than solving it.
Accidents on residential roads have risen.
Traffic on residential roads has increased.

tara.solution: The final sentence is the conclusion; the earlier statements are evidence leading to it. B, D and E are supporting facts, and A is background.

tara.question:
Companies claim that longer opening hours improve customer service. But staff forced to work late become tired and make more errors, and customers report worse experiences in the final hours. Extending opening hours can therefore harm the very service it is meant to improve.

Which of the following is the main conclusion?

options.text: Staff who work late become tired.
Extending opening hours can harm customer service.
Companies want to improve customer service.
Customers report worse experiences late at night.

tara.solution: The conclusion is signalled by 'therefore'; the rest are premises supporting it.

tara.question:
The council plans to cut street lighting at night to save money. A spokesperson argued that this is safe, since most burglaries happen during the day.

Which of the following is an assumption underlying the spokesperson's argument?

options.text: Street lighting is expensive to maintain.
Reducing night lighting will not significantly increase crime or other harms at night.
Burglaries are the most common crime.
The council has a limited budget.

tara.solution: For 'safe' to follow, the argument must assume darkness at night won't raise night-time crime or accidents; deny this and the safety claim collapses.

tara.question:
A commentator argues that since exam results have improved every year, schools must be teaching better than before.

Which of the following is an assumption on which this argument depends?

options.text: The improvement in results reflects better teaching rather than, say, easier exams.

tara.solution: The inference from 'results improved' to 'teaching improved' assumes the results measure teaching quality and are not explained by easier exams or other factors.

tara.question:
Every successful entrepreneur I have read about wakes up before 6 a.m. So if you want to be successful, the key is to start waking up before 6 a.m.

Which of the following best describes the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: It relies on an unrepresentative sample.
It treats a feature that may merely accompany success as though it causes success.
It appeals to the reader's emotions.

tara.solution: The argument assumes early rising causes success, when it may just correlate with it (or result from other traits)—mistaking correlation for cause.

tara.question:
My opponent argues that we should invest more in flood defences. But he owns a house near the river, so his argument should be dismissed.

Which of the following best describes the flaw in this argument?

options.text: It generalises from too few cases.
It rejects a claim by attacking the person making it rather than its merits.

tara.solution: The argument dismisses the proposal because of who makes it (and their interest), not by addressing whether the proposal is sound—an ad hominem.

tara.question:
Either we allow the new factory to be built, or the town will suffer permanent economic decline. We cannot accept decline, so the factory must be built.

Which of the following best identifies the weakness in the argument?

options.text: It assumes there are only two possible outcomes when others may exist.
It attacks the character of opponents.
It relies on a biased sample.

tara.solution: The argument offers a false dilemma: it presents 'factory or permanent decline' as the only options, ignoring other ways the town might avoid decline.

tara.question:
A study found that towns with more libraries have lower crime rates. The researchers concluded that building libraries reduces crime.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the researchers' conclusion?

options.text: Some libraries are open on weekends.
Wealthier towns tend both to build more libraries and to have less crime for other reasons.
Crime rates vary from year to year.
Some towns have very large libraries.

tara.solution: If wealth independently causes both more libraries and less crime, the library–crime link is explained by a third factor, undermining the causal conclusion.

tara.question:
The airline argues that its new booking system is better because complaints about booking have fallen by half since it was introduced.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?

options.text: The airline received an award for customer service.
Over the same period, the airline made it much harder for customers to submit complaints.
The new system was expensive to install.
Some passengers still prefer to book by phone.
The number of flights increased slightly.

tara.solution: If complaints fell because they became harder to submit, the drop no longer shows the system is better—removing the support for the conclusion.

tara.question:
A school introduced a free breakfast programme and, over the following year, attendance improved. The head teacher claims the breakfast caused the improvement.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the head teacher's claim?

options.text: The breakfasts were popular with students.
Comparable schools without the programme saw no change in attendance over the same year.
The programme was funded by donations.
Some students already ate breakfast at home.

tara.solution: A comparison group that saw no change isolates the programme as the likely cause, strengthening the causal claim.

tara.question:
Principle: A person should not be blamed for an outcome they could not reasonably have foreseen or prevented.

Applying this principle, in which case should the person NOT be blamed?

options.text: A driver obeying all rules brakes immediately when a child suddenly darts into the road, but cannot avoid a collision.
A driver who was texting causes a crash.
A shopkeeper knowingly sells food past its safe date and customers fall ill.
A cyclist rides through a red light and hits a pedestrian.
A builder uses materials he knows to be unsafe and a wall collapses.

tara.solution: Only A involves an outcome the person could neither foresee nor prevent; by the principle they should not be blamed. In the others the person could have foreseen or prevented the harm.

tara.question:
If the bridge were unsafe, it would have been closed. It has not been closed. So the bridge is not unsafe.

Which of the following arguments has the same logical structure as the argument above?

options.text: If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was not cancelled. So it did not rain.
If it rains, the match is cancelled. It rained. So the match was cancelled.
The match is cancelled only when it rains. It did not rain. So the match went ahead.
If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was cancelled. So it rained.
It never rains during matches, so matches are never cancelled.

tara.solution: The original is: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P (valid, modus tollens). A matches exactly: if rain then cancelled; not cancelled; so no rain.

tara.question:
Supporters of the ban on advertising unhealthy food to children say it will reduce childhood obesity. Yet children see such adverts mainly through programmes streamed from abroad, which the ban cannot reach. The ban is therefore unlikely to achieve its aim.

Which of the following is the main conclusion?

options.text: The ban aims to reduce childhood obesity.
Children mainly see the adverts through foreign streaming.
The ban is unlikely to achieve its aim.

tara.solution: 'Therefore' marks the conclusion; the point about foreign streaming is the reason supporting it.

tara.question:
The minister said that because the number of people in work has reached a record high, the economy must be healthy.

Which assumption does the minister's argument rely on?

options.text: A record number in work reliably indicates a healthy economy, ignoring factors such as low pay or underemployment.

tara.solution: Inferring 'healthy economy' from 'record employment' assumes employment numbers capture economic health, overlooking pay, hours or underemployment.

tara.question:
Whenever the school football team wins, the local shop sells more pies the next day. Last Monday the shop sold a record number of pies. So the team must have won on Sunday.

Which of the following best describes the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: It assumes that because one thing follows another, the second must have been caused by the first.
It treats a possible cause of the pie sales as the only possible cause.
It relies on an unrepresentative sample.

tara.solution: A win is only one possible reason for high pie sales; the argument wrongly treats it as the only explanation, ignoring other causes.

tara.question:
A newspaper claims its readers are the best informed, citing a survey in which its own readers rated themselves highly on current affairs.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the newspaper's claim?

options.text: When tested on current affairs, the newspaper's readers scored no higher than average.

tara.solution: Self-rating is unreliable; an objective test showing no advantage undermines the claim that the readers are best informed.

tara.question:
A politician argues that lowering the speed limit will save lives, because slower cars cause less severe injuries in a crash.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?

options.text: In areas where the limit was lowered, the number of serious injuries fell significantly.
Cars are safer than they used to be.
Speed limits are set by law.

tara.solution: Evidence that lowering the limit actually reduced serious injuries directly supports the claim that it saves lives.

tara.question:
All the members of the committee I have spoken to support the proposal. Therefore the whole committee supports it.

Which of the following best describes the weakness in this argument?

options.text: It generalises to the whole committee from possibly only some of its members.

tara.solution: The speaker has only spoken to some members but concludes about all of them—an unwarranted generalisation from a partial sample.

tara.question:
The report recommends replacing the old boilers because doing so will cut heating bills. But the new boilers cost far more to install than the bills they would save over their lifetime.

Which of the following is the main conclusion implicitly supported by the second sentence?

options.text: The old boilers should be replaced.
Replacing the boilers is not, overall, worth the cost.

tara.solution: The second sentence gives a reason cutting against the recommendation, supporting the implicit conclusion that replacement is not worthwhile overall.

tara.question:
Principle: People should be free to take risks that affect only themselves.

Which of the following judgements best conforms to this principle?

options.text: An adult who fully understands the risks should be allowed to climb a dangerous mountain alone.
A factory should be allowed to release toxic fumes over a neighbourhood.
A driver should be allowed to drive drunk on public roads.
A person should be allowed to set fires that spread to others' homes.
A company should be allowed to sell unsafe toys.

tara.solution: Only A involves a risk affecting only the person taking it; the others impose risks on other people, which the principle does not license.

tara.question:
Since the introduction of the new software, the team has completed more tasks each week. The manager concludes that the software has made the team more productive.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the manager's conclusion?

options.text: The team likes the new software.
At the same time as the software was introduced, two extra staff joined the team.
The software was recommended by experts.

tara.solution: If extra staff arrived simultaneously, the increased output may be due to them rather than the software, weakening the causal claim.

tara.question:
A charity states that donations rose after it launched an advertising campaign, proving that the campaign was effective.

Which of the following is an assumption the charity's reasoning depends on?

options.text: The rise in donations was due to the campaign rather than to some other cause.

tara.solution: Concluding the campaign was effective assumes it, rather than an unrelated factor (a news event, the season), caused the rise in donations.

tara.question:
If a student has revised properly, they will pass. Priya has not passed. So Priya cannot have revised properly.

Which of the following arguments has the same structure as the one above?

options.text: If a plant is watered, it grows. This plant has not grown. So it was not watered.
If a plant is watered, it grows. This plant was watered. So it grew.
If a plant is watered, it grows. This plant grew. So it was watered.
Plants grow only in summer. It is not summer. So plants are not growing.
This plant grew, so it must be summer.

tara.solution: Original: if P then Q; not Q; so not P (modus tollens). A has exactly this form: if watered then grows; not grown; so not watered.

tara.question:
The manager says the office should return to full-time in-person work, because the most productive week last year was one when everyone happened to be in the office.

Which of the following best describes the weakness in the manager's reasoning?

options.text: It draws a general conclusion from a single, possibly untypical, week.

tara.solution: One exceptional week is a very small and possibly unrepresentative sample from which to conclude that full-time in-person work is generally more productive.

tara.question:
Electric cars produce no exhaust emissions, so switching to them is often presented as a clean solution. But the electricity that charges them may be generated by burning coal, and manufacturing their batteries is highly polluting. Whether electric cars are truly cleaner depends on how the electricity is produced and how the batteries are made.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion?

options.text: Electric cars produce no exhaust emissions.
Whether electric cars are cleaner depends on electricity generation and battery manufacture.
Coal is used to generate electricity.
Electric cars are presented as a clean solution.

tara.solution: The final sentence draws the conclusion; the rest are considerations leading to it.

tara.question:
The library plans to replace its printed books with e-books to save space. But many of its users are elderly and unfamiliar with e-readers, and the library's aim is to serve its community. Replacing all printed books could therefore work against the library's own purpose.

Which of the following is the main conclusion?

options.text: Replacing all printed books could work against the library's purpose.
The library aims to serve its community.
Some users are unfamiliar with e-readers.

tara.solution: 'Therefore' signals the conclusion; the other statements are premises.

tara.question:
Advocates say driverless cars will make roads safer because they remove human error. Yet driverless cars must still share the road with human drivers, cyclists and pedestrians, whose behaviour is unpredictable. Removing human error from one vehicle does not remove it from the road.

Which of the following is the main conclusion?

options.text: Driverless cars remove human error from one vehicle.
Removing human error from one vehicle does not remove it from the road.
Driverless cars will make roads safer.
Cars share the road with cyclists.

tara.solution: The last sentence is the author's conclusion, countering the advocates' claim in the first.

tara.question:
A gym advertises that members who attend more than three times a week are fitter than average. It concludes that attending more than three times a week will make you fitter than average.

Which assumption does the gym's conclusion depend on?

options.text: Frequent attendance causes greater fitness, rather than fit people choosing to attend more often.

tara.solution: The move from a correlation to a recommendation assumes attendance causes fitness, not that already-fit people attend more.

tara.question:
A council will install speed bumps on a road because a petition signed by 200 residents asked for them. It assumes this shows the measure is wanted by the community.

Which of the following is an assumption underlying the council's reasoning?

options.text: The 200 signatories are representative of the wider community's wishes.

tara.solution: Treating 200 signatures as showing what the community wants assumes those signatories represent the community rather than a vocal minority.

tara.question:
A firm argues that its training course is excellent because 95% of those who complete it pass the professional exam.

Which assumption is required for this to show the course is excellent?

options.text: Those who complete the course would not have passed at a similar rate without it.

tara.solution: A high pass rate shows the course is effective only if completers wouldn't have passed anyway; perhaps only strong candidates finish.

tara.question:
Since I started wearing my lucky socks, my team has won five games in a row. The socks are clearly bringing us luck.

Which of the following best describes the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: It treats coincidence, or an unrelated cause, as though it were the cause of the wins.
It relies on a false dilemma.
It generalises from a large sample.

tara.solution: The argument assumes the socks caused the wins, ignoring coincidence or the team's actual form—mistaking correlation for cause.

tara.question:
The proposal to fund music lessons in schools was put forward by a well-known musician. Since she obviously stands to gain from more people valuing music, we should ignore her proposal.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: It dismisses the proposal by pointing to the proposer's interest rather than assessing the proposal itself.
It generalises from too few cases.

tara.solution: The proposal is rejected because of who made it and their interest, not on its merits—an ad hominem.

tara.question:
We must either ban all cars from the city centre or accept that it will become unbreathable. Since we cannot let it become unbreathable, all cars must be banned.

Which of the following best identifies the weakness?

options.text: It assumes there are only two options when intermediate measures are possible.
It relies on an unrepresentative sample.

tara.solution: A false dilemma: it ignores intermediate options such as restrictions, charges, or cleaner vehicles.

tara.question:
This diet must work: it is recommended in a book that has sold millions of copies.

Which of the following best describes the flaw in this argument?

options.text: It treats popularity as evidence of correctness.
It generalises from a single case.

tara.solution: High sales show popularity, not that the diet works—an appeal to popularity.

tara.question:
Our new manager cannot be trusted to run the finance team: after all, she failed her driving test twice.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: It draws a conclusion about one ability from an unrelated failure.
It relies on a biased sample.

tara.solution: Failing a driving test is irrelevant to competence in finance; the argument connects unrelated matters.

tara.question:
A town introduced free parking and shortly afterwards its shops reported higher sales. The mayor concluded that free parking boosted the local economy.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the mayor's conclusion?

options.text: Free parking is popular with drivers.
A large new employer opened in the town in the same month, bringing many workers.
The car park has many spaces.

tara.solution: A simultaneous new employer offers an alternative cause for the sales rise, undermining the free-parking explanation.

tara.question:
A company claims its staff are happier since it introduced an open-plan office, citing that fewer employees have complained to managers.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this claim?

options.text: Employees now sit closer to their managers and are more reluctant to complain.
Some staff prefer working from home.

tara.solution: If proximity to managers deters complaints, fewer complaints need not mean greater happiness—removing the support.

tara.question:
A study reports that people who drink red wine live longer, and concludes that red wine promotes longevity.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the conclusion?

options.text: Red-wine drinkers in the study were, on average, wealthier and had better healthcare.

tara.solution: If wealth and healthcare explain both the wine-drinking and the longevity, the causal claim about wine is undermined.

tara.question:
A politician says her policies have worked because unemployment has fallen since she took office.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this claim?

options.text: Unemployment fell at the same rate in neighbouring countries with very different policies.

tara.solution: If unemployment fell equally where different policies applied, her policies are not shown to be the cause.

tara.question:
A hospital introduced a new hand-washing protocol, and infection rates then fell. The staff claim the protocol caused the fall.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen this claim?

options.text: Wards that did not adopt the protocol saw no change in infection rates over the same period.
The protocol was easy to follow.
Staff were trained in the protocol.

tara.solution: A comparison group without the protocol and without change isolates the protocol as the likely cause.

tara.question:
A teacher believes that reading aloud daily improves pupils' vocabulary, because her class that read aloud scored highly on a vocabulary test.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen this belief?

options.text: A similar class that did not read aloud scored much lower on the same test.
The test was taken in the morning.

tara.solution: A comparable class without the practice scoring lower supports the claim that reading aloud, not some other factor, raised scores.

tara.question:
Principle: People should bear the costs of risks they choose to take, provided those risks fall only on themselves.

Which judgement best conforms to this principle?

options.text: A solo sailor who ignores a storm warning and needs rescue should pay the cost of the rescue.
A pedestrian hit by a speeding driver should pay for their own treatment.
A child injured by a faulty toy should bear the cost.
A worker harmed by unsafe machinery should pay for repairs.
A passenger in a crash caused by the driver should pay the damages.

tara.solution: Only A involves a freely chosen risk falling on the risk-taker; the principle then says they should bear its cost.

tara.question:
Principle: A rule is fair only if it can be applied consistently to everyone, including those who make it.

Which of the following best conforms to this principle?

options.text: A committee sets a rule that all members, themselves included, must declare any conflict of interest.
A manager exempts himself from the dress code he imposes on staff.
Lawmakers pass a tax from which they alone are exempt.
A teacher bans phones but uses hers freely in class.
A club's founders are excused from the fees others must pay.

tara.solution: Only A applies the rule to its makers as well; the others exempt the rule-makers, violating the principle.

tara.question:
All the cakes that sold out were chocolate. This cake is chocolate, so it will sell out.

Which of the following arguments is flawed in the same way?

options.text: All the students who passed revised. Sam revised, so Sam will pass.
All who passed revised. Sam passed, so Sam revised.
No one who revised failed. Sam failed, so Sam did not revise.
Everyone who revised passed. Sam did not revise, so Sam failed.
Sam passed and revised, so revising guarantees passing.

tara.solution: The original wrongly infers 'chocolate ⇒ sells out' from 'sold out ⇒ chocolate'. A repeats this: from 'passed ⇒ revised' it wrongly infers 'revised ⇒ pass'.

tara.question:
If the alarm had been set, it would have rung. It did ring. So the alarm had been set.

Which of the following has the same (flawed) structure?

options.text: If it snowed, school would close. School closed. So it snowed.
If it snowed, school would close. It snowed. So school closed.
If it snowed, school would close. School did not close. So it did not snow.
School closes only when it snows. It did not snow. So school did not close.
It snowed, so school will close.

tara.solution: The original affirms the consequent (if P then Q; Q; so P)—invalid. A has the same invalid form.

tara.question:
Since introducing background music, the café reports that customers stay longer. The owner concludes the music makes customers want to stay.

Which assumption does this conclusion depend on?

options.text: The longer stays are due to the music rather than to some other change made at the same time.

tara.solution: Concluding the music caused longer stays assumes nothing else (new seating, menu, weather) explains the change.

tara.question:
A report notes that neighbourhoods with more CCTV cameras record more reported crime, and concludes that CCTV increases crime.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: More cameras may lead to more crimes being detected and reported, not more crimes occurring.

tara.solution: Higher reported crime may reflect better detection by cameras, not a real increase—so the causal conclusion is unwarranted.

tara.question:
A shopkeeper argues that since his most expensive coffee is his best seller, customers must prefer more expensive coffee.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?

options.text: The expensive coffee is the only large-sized option, which is why most people buy it.
The shop is busy in the morning.

tara.solution: If it sells because it is the only large size, its popularity is not evidence that customers prefer higher prices.

tara.question:
The minister claims the new curriculum is a success because national test scores rose the year it was introduced.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the minister's claim?

options.text: The tests taken that year were found to be easier than in previous years.
Teachers were trained in the new curriculum.

tara.solution: If the tests were easier, higher scores need not reflect a better curriculum, undermining the success claim.

tara.question:
A commentator argues that reading fiction makes people more empathetic, citing that keen fiction readers score highly on empathy tests.

Which of the following is an assumption of this argument?

options.text: Reading fiction increases empathy, rather than empathetic people being drawn to fiction.

tara.solution: The causal claim assumes fiction causes empathy, not that empathetic people simply prefer fiction.

tara.question:
If a bridge is well maintained, it will not collapse. The old bridge collapsed. Therefore it was not well maintained.

Which of the following has the same (valid) structure?

options.text: If a plant is healthy, it will not wilt. This plant wilted. So it was not healthy.
If a plant is healthy, it will not wilt. This plant is healthy. So it will not wilt.
If a plant is healthy, it will not wilt. This plant did not wilt. So it is healthy.
A plant wilts only if neglected. It was not neglected. So it did not wilt.
This plant wilted, so all plants wilt.

tara.solution: Original: if P then not Q; Q; so not P (valid modus tollens). A matches exactly.

tara.question:
A newspaper claims the economy is booming because the stock market has reached a record high.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this claim?

options.text: The stock market can rise even when wages fall and unemployment grows.

tara.solution: If the market can rise while ordinary economic conditions worsen, a record high does not show the economy is booming.

tara.question:
A school claims its pupils are exceptionally talented, pointing out that its entrance exam is extremely selective.

Which of the following best describes the weakness in using exam results later to prove the school teaches well?

options.text: Strong later results may reflect the pupils' ability on entry rather than the school's teaching.

tara.solution: If only able pupils are admitted, their later success may be due to their ability, not the teaching—so results don't prove good teaching.

tara.question:
A manager says overtime must be increasing productivity, because the month with the most overtime also had the highest output.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: A single month's coincidence of overtime and output does not establish that one caused the other.

tara.solution: One month in which both were high does not show overtime caused the output; it may be coincidence or a shared cause.

tara.question:
A charity argues that people are becoming more generous, because the total amount donated rose last year.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?

options.text: The population and average incomes both grew substantially last year.

tara.solution: If there were more, richer people, a higher total need not mean each person is more generous—weakening the claim.

tara.question:
Principle: One should not be praised for an achievement that was entirely due to luck.

Which judgement best conforms to this principle?

options.text: A lottery winner should not be praised for their 'financial success'.
A student who studied hard and passed should not be praised.
An athlete who trained for years should not be praised for winning.
A scientist who worked carefully should not be credited with a discovery.
A writer who spent years on a novel deserves no praise.

tara.solution: Only A is an outcome purely due to luck; the principle then says praise is inappropriate. The others involved effort.

tara.question:
A blogger insists that a claim must be false because it is believed only by a small minority.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: It treats the number of believers as a test of truth.

tara.solution: How many people hold a belief is not evidence of whether it is true—an appeal to (un)popularity.

tara.question:
Supporters argue that lowering the voting age will engage young people in politics, because countries that lowered it saw higher youth turnout at the next election.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?

options.text: Those countries also ran large, one-off campaigns to register young voters that year.
The voting age varies by country.

tara.solution: If special campaigns drove the turnout, the rise cannot be attributed to lowering the voting age itself.

tara.question:
A firm concludes that its adverts are effective because sales rose during the advertising campaign.

Which assumption does this conclusion rely on?

options.text: The rise in sales was caused by the adverts rather than by other factors such as the season.
The adverts were seen by many people.

tara.solution: Concluding the adverts were effective assumes they, not seasonal demand or other causes, produced the rise in sales.

tara.question:
The council argues that the new cycle lane is unnecessary because a survey found most road users do not cycle.

Which of the following best describes the weakness in this reasoning?

options.text: Few may cycle precisely because there is no safe lane, so current numbers understate potential demand.

tara.solution: Measuring cycling under current unsafe conditions may understate how many would cycle if a lane existed—so low numbers don't settle the matter.

tara.question:
A columnist argues that because two events happened in the same week, one must have caused the other.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: Events occurring close in time need not be causally related.
It generalises from a small sample.

tara.solution: Temporal proximity alone does not establish causation; the events may be unrelated or share a common cause.

tara.question:
A restaurant claims its food is the best in town because it has the longest queue.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this claim?

options.text: The queue is long only because the restaurant is very small and serves slowly.
The restaurant is popular with tourists.

tara.solution: If the queue reflects slow service in a tiny venue rather than quality, its length is not evidence that the food is best.

tara.question:
A study finds that students who use laptops in lectures get lower grades, and concludes that laptops harm learning.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the conclusion?

options.text: Students who were already struggling were the most likely to use laptops to look things up.

tara.solution: If weaker students self-select into laptop use, the lower grades may reflect prior struggle, not harm caused by laptops.

tara.question:
A politician argues: 'My critics say the policy has failed, but they have always opposed me, so their criticism is worthless.'

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: It dismisses the criticism by pointing to the critics' motives instead of addressing whether the policy failed.
It generalises from a small sample.

tara.solution: Longstanding opposition does not make a criticism false; the argument attacks the critics rather than the point—an ad hominem.

tara.question:
A firm notes that its highest-paid employees are also its most productive, and concludes that paying people more makes them more productive.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this conclusion?

options.text: The firm's policy is to pay its already-most-productive employees the most.

tara.solution: If high pay follows from being productive, the causation runs the other way, undermining 'pay makes people productive'.

tara.question:
Because the medicine relieved my headache within an hour, it must have been the medicine that cured it.

Which of the following best describes the weakness in this reasoning?

options.text: The headache might have faded on its own in that time.

tara.solution: Many headaches subside naturally; recovery after taking the medicine doesn't establish that the medicine caused it.

tara.question:
Everyone I asked at the tennis club supports building a new court, so the whole town must support it.

Which of the following best describes the flaw?

options.text: It generalises from a group with a special interest to the whole town.

tara.solution: Tennis club members are hardly representative of the town on this issue; the sample is biased toward supporters.

tara.question:
A company argues that its product is safe because no customer has ever reported being harmed by it.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?

options.text: The company provides no way for customers to report harm.

tara.solution: Absence of reports may reflect the absence of a reporting channel, not the absence of harm—an appeal to ignorance.

tara.question:
A council states that its recycling scheme is working because the amount of recycling collected has doubled.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this claim?

options.text: The council also doubled the number of households in the collection area.

tara.solution: If the number of households doubled too, the increase may reflect more participants, not a more effective scheme.

tara.question:
Amber case. A scholarship requires a maths score above 70 and an interview score of at least 7. Art scores are recorded but are not used.

Aster: maths 73, interview 8, art 56
Birch: maths 68, interview 8, art 63
Cedar: maths 76, interview 5, art 70
Dahlia: maths 68, interview 8, art 77
Elm: maths 76, interview 5, art 84

Who qualifies?
tara.solution: Aster is the only candidate satisfying both relevant thresholds; the art score is irrelevant.

tara.question:
Amber case. A traveller needs to arrive by 09:30, make no more than one change, and then chooses the cheapest eligible service.

Aster: arrives 9:40, 0 change(s), fare £27
Birch: arrives 9:45, 0 change(s), fare £28
Cedar: arrives 9:25, 1 change(s), fare £24
Dahlia: arrives 9:15, 0 change(s), fare £30
Elm: arrives 10:00, 2 change(s), fare £31

Which service should be chosen?
tara.solution: Cedar meets both journey constraints and is the cheapest eligible service.

tara.question:
Amber case. A club needs 50 identical folders. It can spend at most £10 per folder. Supplier ratings are not part of the decision.

Aster: stock 55, price £12, rating 4/5
Birch: stock 35, price £9, rating 5/5
Cedar: stock 55, price £14, rating 3/5
Dahlia: stock 60, price £8, rating 4/5
Elm: stock 55, price £16, rating 5/5

Which supplier meets the requirements?
tara.solution: Dahlia has enough stock and stays within the unit budget; the rating is irrelevant.

tara.question:
Amber case. An event expects 130 guests. The venue must be within 6 km, and the organiser chooses the cheapest venue that satisfies both conditions.

Aster: 110 seats, 5 km away, £470
Birch: 150 seats, 8 km away, £490
Cedar: 150 seats, 5 km away, £510
Dahlia: 150 seats, 5 km away, £530
Elm: 140 seats, 3 km away, £420

Which venue should be booked?
tara.solution: Elm has enough seats, is close enough, and has the lowest cost among eligible venues.

tara.question:
Amber case. A pupil's bag holds at most 6 books. Only books needed before break matter because the pupil can visit the locker then.

Monday: 5 books before break, 3 after lunch
Tuesday: 9 books before break, 5 after lunch
Wednesday: 7 books before break, 2 after lunch
Thursday: 8 books before break, 4 after lunch
Friday: 9 books before break, 6 after lunch

On which day is no pre-break locker visit needed?
tara.solution: Monday is the only day with no more than 6 books needed before break; afternoon books are irrelevant.

tara.question: A cyclist rides to a town at $30$ km/h and returns along the same road at $60$ km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey?
tara.solution: Average speed $=\dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}=\dfrac{2\cdot30\cdot60}{90}=40$ km/h (not the arithmetic mean).

tara.question: A coat priced at £$200$ is reduced by $10\%$, and the reduced price is then cut by a further $20\%$ in a sale. What is the final price?
tara.solution: Successive discounts multiply: £$200\times\frac{9}{10}\times\frac{4}{5}=£144$ (a $10\%$ then $20\%$ cut is not a $30\%$ cut).

tara.question: One tap fills a tank in $4$ hours and another fills it in $6$ hours. How long do they take to fill it together?
tara.solution: Combined rate $=\tfrac1{4}+\tfrac1{6}$ tanks/hour; time $=\dfrac1{1/4+1/6}=\frac{12}{5}$ hours.

tara.question: A large cube of side $3$ units is painted on all outer faces and then cut into unit cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
tara.solution: Two-face cubes lie along edges (excluding corners): $12(n-2)=12(3-2)=12.$

tara.question: A cube of side $3$ is painted and cut into unit cubes. How many have exactly one painted face?
tara.solution: One-face cubes lie on faces (excluding edges): $6(n-2)^2=6(3-2)^2=6.$

tara.question: A quantity changes from $200$ to $250$. What is the percentage change?
tara.solution: Percentage change $=\dfrac{250-200}{200}\times100=25\%.$

tara.question: An item bought for £$50$ is sold for £$75$. What is the percentage profit or loss?
tara.solution: Profit $\%=\dfrac{75-50}{50}\times100=50\%$ (negative means a loss).

tara.question: After a $20\%$ reduction, a jacket costs £$120$. What was its original price?
Two trains start $300$ km apart and travel toward each other at $40$ km/h and $60$ km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
tara.solution: Closing speed $=40+60=100$ km/h; time $=\dfrac{300}{100}=3$ hours.

tara.question: A group of $10$ students averages $60$ marks and another group of $20$ students averages $90$. What is the overall average?
tara.solution: Overall $=\dfrac{10\cdot60+20\cdot90}{30}=80$ (weighted, not simple, mean).

tara.question: A box measures $10\times3\times2$. What is its volume?
tara.solution: Volume $=10\times3\times2=60.$

tara.question: A recipe for $8$ people needs $200$ g of flour. How much is needed for $2$ people?
tara.solution: Scale by $\tfrac{2}{8}$: $200\times\tfrac{2}{8}=50$ g.

tara.question: Amber case. A machine records outputs in the ratio $2:3:5:8$. Which record has exactly the same relative pattern?
tara.solution: Multiplying every term of $2:3:5:8$ by 2 gives 4, 6, 10, 16.

tara.question: Amber case. A route follows the directions N, E, E, S. Which route has the same shape after a rotation, without reflection?
tara.solution: E, S, S, W preserves every turn and segment pattern under rotation.

tara.question: Amber case. Four teams have scores $11, 5, 9, 3$. Which list gives the same ranking from highest to lowest across its four positions?
tara.solution: The first position is highest, the third is second, the second is third, and the fourth is lowest in both lists.

tara.question: Amber case. A reading rises by 3, falls by 2, then stays unchanged. Which four-reading record has the same pattern?
tara.solution: 11, 14, 12, 12 changes by $+3,-2,0$ in that order.

tara.question: Amber case. Three categories occur in the ratio $2:3:5$. Which data set would produce the same sector proportions in a pie chart?
tara.solution: 4, 6, 10 is a common multiple of $2:3:5$, so the proportions match.

tara.question: How much is saved on a £$80$ item reduced by $10\%$?
tara.solution: Saving $=80\times10/100=£8.$

tara.question: A film starts $50$ minutes after $1$ h $45 min past midnight. How many minutes past midnight does it start?
tara.solution: Start $=1\times60+45+50=155$ minutes past midnight.

tara.question: A rectangle measures $8$ by $7$. What is its area?
tara.solution: Area $=8\times7=56.$

tara.question: A rectangle measures $8$ by $7$. What is its perimeter?
tara.solution: Perimeter $=2(8+7)=30.$

tara.question: Find the mean of $\{12, 15, 9, 6, 18\}$.
Cobalt case. A machine records outputs in the ratio $2:3:5:8$. Which record has exactly the same relative pattern?
tara.solution: Multiplying every term of $2:3:5:8$ by 4 gives 8, 12, 20, 32.

tara.question: Cobalt case. A route follows the directions S, W, W, N. Which route has the same shape after a rotation, without reflection?
tara.solution: W, N, N, E preserves every turn and segment pattern under rotation.

tara.question: Cobalt case. Four teams have scores $13, 7, 11, 5$. Which list gives the same ranking from highest to lowest across its four positions?
tara.solution: The first position is highest, the third is second, the second is third, and the fourth is lowest in both lists.

tara.question: Cobalt case. A reading rises by 3, falls by 2, then stays unchanged. Which four-reading record has the same pattern?
tara.solution: 13, 16, 14, 14 changes by $+3,-2,0$ in that order.

tara.question: Cobalt case. Three categories occur in the ratio $2:3:5$. Which data set would produce the same sector proportions in a pie chart?
tara.solution: 8, 12, 20 is a common multiple of $2:3:5$, so the proportions match.
