essayPrompts.title: Academic Writing Task 2

parts.label: Task 2
parts.question: Some people believe universities should prioritise courses that lead directly to employment. Others believe their purpose is broader. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
parts.solutionOutline: Define what 'prioritise' means, present the strongest case for employability and for broader education, then state a qualified position supported by reasons and examples.

ielts.fullSolution: There is no single correct view. High-band work answers every part, develops both positions fairly, maintains a clear thesis and uses examples as evidence rather than decoration.

ielts.context: Speaking Part 2 rehearsal. Prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes. Type a faithful transcript or use the AI interview room to practise aloud.

parts.label: Long turn
parts.question: Describe a skill you learned outside school. Say what it was, how you learned it, what was difficult, and explain why it remains useful.
parts.solutionOutline: Sustain a coherent two-minute account, sequence events, add specific detail and explain significance. Natural self-correction is acceptable.

ielts.fullSolution: Assessment focuses on fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation. A memorised script is not the goal.

ielts.context: Speaking Part 3 rehearsal. Respond analytically, extending each answer with reasons, distinctions and examples.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: How has technology changed the way young people learn practical skills?
parts.solutionOutline: Give a balanced comparison, distinguish access from mastery, and support claims.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Which skills are difficult to teach online, and why?
parts.solutionOutline: Identify concrete skill properties such as tacit feedback, safety or physical coordination.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Should governments fund lifelong learning for adults?
parts.solutionOutline: State criteria, weigh public benefit and cost, and reach a qualified view.

ielts.fullSolution: Strong responses move beyond personal anecdotes, compare alternatives and explain causal links while remaining spontaneous and intelligible.

csat.context: A robot starts at 1. At each step it may double its current number or add 3.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Find a shortest sequence of operations that reaches 29.
parts.solutionOutline: Work backwards: inverse moves are subtract 3 and, for even values, halve.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Describe an algorithm that finds a shortest sequence to any reachable target n, and justify why it is shortest.
parts.solutionOutline: Use breadth-first search on states; the first visit occurs at minimum number of edges.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Give a target that is not reachable and prove it.
parts.solutionOutline: Track residues or parity from the start and establish an invariant.

csat.fullSolution: A breadth-first search explores all values at distance 0, then 1, then 2. Keeping predecessors reconstructs a shortest path. Reachability claims must be established with an invariant, not a failed search alone.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: A list of n distinct numbers is repeatedly split in half until singletons remain, then merged in sorted order. How many comparison levels are used when n=2^k?
parts.solutionOutline: There are k splitting/merging levels.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Show that each level uses at most n comparisons.
parts.solutionOutline: The merged sublists have total length n; each merge uses fewer comparisons than its total length.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Deduce an upper bound and compare it with checking every pair.
parts.solutionOutline: At most nk = n log2 n versus n(n-1)/2.

csat.fullSolution: For n=2^k there are k merge levels. Each handles every element once and uses fewer than n comparisons, giving fewer than n log2 n comparisons overall.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Prove that if n^2 is even then n is even.
parts.solutionOutline: Use the contrapositive: an odd n=2k+1 has odd square.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Explain why checking many examples is not a proof.
parts.solutionOutline: Finite checks do not cover an unbounded domain; distinguish evidence from deduction.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: State and prove the corresponding claim for divisibility by 3.
parts.solutionOutline: Use residues 0,1,2 modulo 3; squares are 0 or 1.

csat.fullSolution: The contrapositive of the first claim follows from (2k+1)^2=4k(k+1)+1. Modulo 3, only residue 0 has square divisible by 3.

csat.context: One of three programs A, B and C contains a fault. Tests report: T1 says A or B is faulty; T2 says B is not faulty; T3 says C is faulty. Exactly one test report is false.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Determine the faulty program, or show that the information is insufficient.
parts.solutionOutline: Evaluate each single-fault case against all three reports.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Write the condition using Boolean variables.
parts.solutionOutline: Use exactly-one constraints and truth values for T1-T3.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Change one report so the fault is uniquely determined, and justify your change.
parts.solutionOutline: Propose a predicate and verify all cases.

csat.fullSolution: A complete answer tabulates A-only, B-only and C-only. The second part should distinguish the world variables from whether a report is true.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: How many binary strings of length 8 contain exactly three 1s?
parts.solutionOutline: Choose the three positions: C(8,3).

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: How many contain no adjacent 1s?
parts.solutionOutline: Shift selected positions or use gaps; choose 3 positions from 6 adjusted slots.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Generalise to length n with exactly k non-adjacent 1s.
parts.solutionOutline: Map positions i_j to i_j-(j-1), giving C(n-k+1,k).

csat.fullSolution: There are C(8,3)=56 unrestricted strings. Non-adjacent choices correspond bijectively to choosing k positions among n-k+1, hence C(n-k+1,k).

csat.context: A password is a string over {A,B,C} in which no two adjacent symbols are equal.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Count passwords of length n.
parts.solutionOutline: Three choices initially and two thereafter.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Count those of length n that start and end with A.
parts.solutionOutline: Set up two states: ends in A versus ends outside A, then solve the recurrence.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Explain how the method changes for an alphabet of q symbols.
parts.solutionOutline: Use the same state recurrence with q-1 and q-2 transitions.

csat.fullSolution: The unrestricted count is 3·2^(n-1). For fixed endpoints, a two-state recurrence or a 2x2 transition matrix gives a closed form; the reasoning matters more than memorising it.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Prove that every finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves.
parts.solutionOutline: Take a longest simple path; neither endpoint can have another neighbour.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Show that deleting a leaf from a tree leaves a tree.
parts.solutionOutline: Connectivity remains and no cycle is created.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Use induction to show a tree with n vertices has n-1 edges.
parts.solutionOutline: Delete a leaf and apply the induction hypothesis.

csat.fullSolution: Endpoints of a longest path must have degree one. Leaf deletion preserves connectedness and acyclicity, enabling induction on the vertex count.

csat.context: Six computers are connected so that each computer is directly linked to exactly two others.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: List the possible shapes if the network is connected.
parts.solutionOutline: A finite connected 2-regular graph is a cycle.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Remove the connected assumption. Classify all possible networks.
parts.solutionOutline: Every component is a cycle of length at least 3; partition 6 accordingly.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Give an O(n) procedure to determine the components.
parts.solutionOutline: Depth-first or breadth-first traversal visits each vertex and edge once.

csat.fullSolution: Every component of a finite 2-regular simple graph is a cycle. With six vertices, the possibilities are C6 or two disjoint triangles.

csat.context: A lift serves floors 0 to 20. Moving one floor costs one unit of time; opening and closing doors costs four units per stop.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Compare serving requests 3, 7 and 12 in ascending order with returning to floor 0 after every request.
parts.solutionOutline: Calculate travel plus stop costs under both policies.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: State two assumptions hidden in this model and explain their effect.
parts.solutionOutline: Examples: equal travel time, no capacity, all requests known, no boarding time.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Propose a better objective than total time when passengers wait unequally.
parts.solutionOutline: Consider average wait, maximum wait or weighted delay and discuss trade-offs.

csat.fullSolution: A good model answer computes consistently, exposes assumptions and recognises that optimisation depends on the chosen fairness objective.

csat.context: Messages spread through a network. In each round, every informed user sends the message to two previously uninformed users if possible.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Give an upper bound on the number informed after r rounds.
parts.solutionOutline: At most 3^r if each informed user recruits two new users each round, with the initial user at r=0.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Explain why real networks may grow much more slowly.
parts.solutionOutline: Overlapping contacts, degree limits, repeated targets and disconnected regions.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Define a graph model and an algorithm to simulate one round.
parts.solutionOutline: Specify vertices, edges, informed set and update simultaneously; discuss order effects.

csat.fullSolution: The idealised recurrence I_(r+1)<=3I_r gives I_r<=3^r, capped by population. A robust simulation separates the current informed set from next-round additions.

csat.context: A warehouse robot must visit every marked square in a rectangular grid. It may move one square north, south, east or west, and some squares are blocked.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Describe how breadth-first search can find a shortest route from the start to one marked square.
parts.solutionOutline: Treat open squares as vertices and legal moves as edges; BFS first reaches a square at minimum distance.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Explain why repeatedly visiting the nearest remaining mark need not minimise the complete route.
parts.solutionOutline: Give a configuration where a locally nearest mark leaves two distant regions to be crossed inefficiently.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: State one exact approach for a small number k of marked squares and discuss its cost.
parts.solutionOutline: Compute pairwise shortest paths, then use subset dynamic programming over visited marks in O(2^k k^2).

csat.fullSolution: BFS solves each unweighted shortest-path subproblem. The full visit-all problem needs global state; subset dynamic programming is exact for small k but exponential in the number of marks.

csat.context: A system grants access when (P and Q) or (not P and R) is true.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Construct a complete truth table for the access rule.
parts.solutionOutline: List all eight assignments and evaluate both conjunctions before the disjunction.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Show that Q or R being true is necessary but not sufficient for access.
parts.solutionOutline: Prove necessity from the two branches, then give a counterexample for sufficiency.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Design an equivalent decision tree that asks P first and justify the equivalence.
parts.solutionOutline: If P is true, test Q; otherwise test R. Match both branches to the Boolean expression.

csat.fullSolution: Conditioning on P reduces the rule to Q when P is true and R when P is false. The truth table and decision tree must agree on all eight inputs.

csat.context: A code consists of four distinct digits chosen from 0 to 9. The first digit cannot be 0.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Count all valid codes.
parts.solutionOutline: Choose the first digit in 9 ways, then 9, 8 and 7 remaining choices.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Count valid codes containing exactly one even digit.
parts.solutionOutline: Separate whether the single even digit is zero and whether it occupies the first position.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Explain how inclusion-exclusion could count codes containing at least one of the digits 1, 2 and 3.
parts.solutionOutline: Define events for containing each specified digit and subtract pair intersections before adding the triple intersection.

csat.fullSolution: The unrestricted count is 9x9x8x7. Parts (ii) and (iii) require careful treatment of the leading-zero restriction rather than treating all positions symmetrically.

csat.context: Courses are vertices of a graph. Two courses are joined when at least one student takes both, so joined courses cannot have exams at the same time.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Explain why a valid timetable corresponds to a proper vertex colouring.
parts.solutionOutline: Time slots are colours and adjacent courses require different colours.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Show that a graph containing an odd cycle cannot be scheduled in two slots.
parts.solutionOutline: Alternating two colours around an odd cycle forces the final edge to join equal colours.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Describe a greedy scheduling algorithm and explain why its result need not use the fewest slots.
parts.solutionOutline: Process vertices in an order and assign the first available colour; a poor order can introduce avoidable colours.

csat.fullSolution: Graph colouring models the conflict constraint exactly. Odd cycles obstruct two-colourability, while greedy colouring is valid but its colour count depends on vertex order.

csat.context: A video platform chooses which files to keep in a limited cache. A request served from the cache costs 1 unit of time; any other request costs 12 units and loads that file into the cache.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Compare least-recently-used and first-in-first-out on the request sequence A,B,C,A,D,A with cache size 3.
parts.solutionOutline: Track the cache after each request and total the hits and misses for both policies.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Give a request pattern on which one policy clearly outperforms the other.
parts.solutionOutline: Construct and simulate a sequence that revisits a recently used old file after FIFO evicts it.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Identify two assumptions that make this model unrealistic and propose one improved objective.
parts.solutionOutline: Files may differ in size or load cost; requests may have priorities. Minimise weighted delay or total bandwidth rather than misses alone.

csat.fullSolution: A correct answer records cache state, not only the final miss count. The modelling discussion should connect changed assumptions to a revised policy or objective.

csat.context: An array contains n integers. A contiguous segment is called balanced when its sum is zero.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Give a direct O(n^2) method to find a longest balanced segment.
parts.solutionOutline: Try every start and extend the end while maintaining a running sum.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: Design an O(n) expected-time method using prefix sums and a dictionary.
parts.solutionOutline: Equal prefix sums at positions i and j imply the intervening segment sums to zero; store the earliest index for each sum.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: Prove that keeping only the earliest occurrence of each prefix sum is sufficient.
parts.solutionOutline: For any later matching endpoint, the earliest equal prefix gives the longest segment ending there.

csat.fullSolution: Let S_j be the sum before position j. Segment i through j-1 is balanced exactly when S_i=S_j. Recording the earliest index for each prefix sum maximises every candidate length.

caie9709.context: The point representing $z$ lies on $|z-2i|=3$ with $\operatorname{Re}(z)\ge 0$. The transformation is $w=z^*-1$.

parts.question: Sketch and describe fully the locus of $w$.
parts.solutionOutline: 共轭先把圆心 $2i$ 关于实轴反射到 $-2i$，再向左平移 1，所以新圆心为 $-1-2i$、半径为 3。因 $\operatorname{Re}(z)=\operatorname{Re}(z^*)=\operatorname{Re}(w)+1$，限制变为 $\operatorname{Re}(w)\ge-1$。轨迹是该圆的右半圆，端点为 $-1+i$ 与 $-1-5i$，端点包含。

caie9709.fullSolution: 共轭先把圆心 $2i$ 关于实轴反射到 $-2i$，再向左平移 1，所以新圆心为 $-1-2i$、半径为 3。因 $\operatorname{Re}(z)=\operatorname{Re}(z^*)=\operatorname{Re}(w)+1$，限制变为 $\operatorname{Re}(w)\ge-1$。轨迹是该圆的右半圆，端点为 $-1+i$ 与 $-1-5i$，端点包含。

parts.question: Evaluate exactly $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}4\cos x\cos 2x\,dx$.
parts.solutionOutline: 用积化和差 $4\cos x\cos2x=2(\cos3x+\cos x)$。积分为 $[\frac23\sin3x+2\sin x]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac23+1=\frac53$。

caie9709.fullSolution: 用积化和差 $4\cos x\cos2x=2(\cos3x+\cos x)$。积分为 $[\frac23\sin3x+2\sin x]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac23+1=\frac53$。

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: The coefficient of $x^2$ in $(1+kx)^{-1/2}$ is $\frac32$, where $k>0$. Find $k$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Hence find the coefficient of $x^3$ in $(1+x)(1+2x)^{-1/2}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.question: State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid.

caie9709.context: $P(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+ax+1$. It is known that $x-1$ and $x^2+x+1$ are factors of $P(x)$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Find $a$ and $b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Hence factorise $P(x)$ completely over the real numbers.

caie9709.context: $\lambda$ is real and positive, and $z=\dfrac{5+\lambda i}{\lambda+i}$. It is given that $\arg z=\dfrac\pi4$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Find $\lambda$ exactly.
parts.solutionOutline: 乘以 $\lambda-i$ 后，$z=\frac{6\lambda+(\lambda^2-5)i}{\lambda^2+1}$。辐角为 $\pi/4$ 表示实部、虚部相等且为正，故 $\lambda^2-5=6\lambda$。解得 $\lambda=3\pm\sqrt{14}$，由正值条件取 $3+\sqrt{14}$。

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Find $|z|$ in exact form.
parts.solutionOutline: 由 $\lambda^2=6\lambda+5$，实部为 $\frac{6\lambda}{\lambda^2+1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}$，且两分量相等，所以 $|z|=\sqrt2\,\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}=\sqrt2\,\frac{3+\sqrt{14}}{4+\sqrt{14}}$。

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) 乘以 $\lambda-i$ 后，$z=\frac{6\lambda+(\lambda^2-5)i}{\lambda^2+1}$。辐角为 $\pi/4$ 表示实部、虚部相等且为正，故 $\lambda^2-5=6\lambda$。解得 $\lambda=3\pm\sqrt{14}$，由正值条件取 $3+\sqrt{14}$。

(b) 由 $\lambda^2=6\lambda+5$，实部为 $\frac{6\lambda}{\lambda^2+1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}$，且两分量相等，所以 $|z|=\sqrt2\,\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}=\sqrt2\,\frac{3+\sqrt{14}}{4+\sqrt{14}}$。

caie9709.context: The equation $x+\ln x=3$ has a positive root $\alpha$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Show that the equation has exactly one positive root.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Show that $2.20<\alpha<2.21$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.question: Use $x_{n+1}=3-\ln x_n$ with $x_1=2.20$ to find $\alpha$ correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.solutionOutline: 反复代入得到收敛序列，稳定到 $\alpha=2.2079$（4 d.p.）。在根附近 $|g'(x)|=1/x<1$，与收敛一致。

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) 令 $f(x)=x+\ln x-3$。在 $x>0$ 上，$f'(x)=1+1/x>0$，所以至多一根；又 $f(2)<0,f(3)>0$，故恰有一根。

(b) $f(2.20)=2.20+\ln2.20-3<0$，而 $f(2.21)>0$；由连续性根位于两者之间。

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (b)

parts.solutionOutline: [B1] Both moduli are $\sqrt{13}$. [M1] Locate each quadrant. [A1] For $u$, argument $-\tan^{-1}(2/3)$. [A1] For $-u$, argument $\pi-\tan^{-1}(2/3)$.

parts.label: (a)

parts.solutionOutline: [B1] Concentration $S/100$ kg per litre. [M1] Salt leaves at $5S/100$, so $S'=-S/20$. [M1] Separate and integrate: $\ln S=-t/20+C$. [A1] Initial data give $e^C=8$. [A1] $S=8e^{-t/20}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Find the time until the concentration first falls below 0.01 kg per litre.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] $S/100<0.01$ means $8e^{-t/20}<1$. [A1] $t>20\ln8$ minutes; threshold time $20\ln8$.

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) [B1] Concentration $S/100$ kg per litre. [M1] Salt leaves at $5S/100$, so $S'=-S/20$. [M1] Separate and integrate: $\ln S=-t/20+C$. [A1] Initial data give $e^C=8$. [A1] $S=8e^{-t/20}$.

(b) [M1] $S/100<0.01$ means $8e^{-t/20}<1$. [A1] $t>20\ln8$ minutes; threshold time $20\ln8$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Show by differentiation that $F'(x)=2x\cos2x$.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Product and chain rules. [A1] The $\sin2x$ terms cancel, leaving $2x\cos2x$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Hence evaluate $\int_0^{\pi/4}x\cos2x\,dx$ exactly.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Antiderivative $F/2$. [M1] $F(\pi/4)=\pi/4$, $F(0)=1/2$. [A1] Result $\pi/8-1/4$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.question: Deduce $\int_0^{\pi/4}x\sin^2x\,dx$ exactly.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] $\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2$. [M1] Subtract half the previous integral from $\int_0^{\pi/4}x/2\,dx$. [A1] Result $\pi^2/64-\pi/16+1/8$.

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) [M1] Product and chain rules. [A1] The $\sin2x$ terms cancel, leaving $2x\cos2x$.

(b) [M1] Antiderivative $F/2$. [M1] $F(\pi/4)=\pi/4$, $F(0)=1/2$. [A1] Result $\pi/8-1/4$.

(c) [M1] $\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2$. [M1] Subtract half the previous integral from $\int_0^{\pi/4}x/2\,dx$. [A1] Result $\pi^2/64-\pi/16+1/8$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: State the permitted values of x and k, and reduce the equation to a quadratic in x.
parts.solutionOutline: [B1] $1<x<5$, $k>0$. [M1] Combine logs on that domain. [A1] $(x-1)(5-x)=k$, or $(x-3)^2=4-k$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Determine the number of distinct real solutions for every real k. Then solve exactly when k=3.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] On the domain the product is positive with maximum 4 at $x=3$. [A1] Two solutions if $0<k<4$, one if $k=4$, none if $k>4$. [B1] For $k\le0$ the original logarithm is undefined, so no admissible solution. [A1] For $k=3$, $x=2,4$; both pass the log-domain check.

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) [B1] $1<x<5$, $k>0$. [M1] Combine logs on that domain. [A1] $(x-1)(5-x)=k$, or $(x-3)^2=4-k$.

(b) [M1] On the domain the product is positive with maximum 4 at $x=3$. [A1] Two solutions if $0<k<4$, one if $k=4$, none if $k>4$. [B1] For $k\le0$ the original logarithm is undefined, so no admissible solution. [A1] For $k=3$, $x=2,4$; both pass the log-domain check.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Express f(x) as $R\cos(2x-\alpha)$ with $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\pi/2$.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Expand the compound angle. [A1] $R\cos\alpha=4$, $R\sin\alpha=3$, so $R=5$. [A1] $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(3/4)$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Solve f(x)=4 exactly, taking care with the half-open interval.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] $\cos(2x-\alpha)=4/5=\cos\alpha$. [A1] $2x-\alpha=\pm\alpha+2n\pi$ gives $x=0,\alpha$ in the stated interval. [B1] $x=\pi$ is excluded; no other integer n works.

parts.label: (c)
parts.question: For each real c, state the number of distinct solutions of f(x)=c in the interval.
parts.solutionOutline: [B1] A single complete period contains two roots for $-5<c<5$. [B1] One for $c=\pm5$ and none for $|c|>5$, with the right endpoint excluded to avoid double-counting.

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) [M1] Expand the compound angle. [A1] $R\cos\alpha=4$, $R\sin\alpha=3$, so $R=5$. [A1] $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(3/4)$.

(b) [M1] $\cos(2x-\alpha)=4/5=\cos\alpha$. [A1] $2x-\alpha=\pm\alpha+2n\pi$ gives $x=0,\alpha$ in the stated interval. [B1] $x=\pi$ is excluded; no other integer n works.

(c) [B1] A single complete period contains two roots for $-5<c<5$. [B1] One for $c=\pm5$ and none for $|c|>5$, with the right endpoint excluded to avoid double-counting.

parts.question: Show that a root lies between 1 and 2.
parts.solutionOutline: [B1] $f(1)=-1$, $f(2)=7$. [B1] f is continuous, so the sign change gives a root in $(1,2)$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Use the given iteration $x_{n+1}=(3-x_n)^{1/3}$ with $x_1=1$ to calculate $x_2$ and $x_3$ to 4 decimal places. Keep full precision internally.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] $x_2=\sqrt[3]2=1.2599$. [A1] $x_3=\sqrt[3]{3-\sqrt[3]2}=1.2028$. These are iterates, not a claim of a 4-decimal-place root.

caie9709.context: The equation is $x+\ln x=2$, with $x>0$. Two proposed iterations are $g(x)=e^{2-x}$ and $h(x)=(x+2-\ln x)/2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Show that the equation has exactly one root alpha between 1 and 2.
parts.solutionOutline: [B1] $f(1)=-1$, $f(2)=\ln2>0$, and f is continuous. [B1] $f'=1+1/x>0$, hence the root is unique.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Show both rearrangements have alpha as a fixed point. Compare the magnitudes of their derivatives near alpha to explain which iteration is suitable.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Each fixed-point equation rearranges to $x+\ln x=2$. [A1] $g'(\alpha)=-\alpha$, so its magnitude exceeds 1; it is locally unstable. [A1] $h'(x)=(1-1/x)/2$, so on $[1,2]$ it is between 0 and 1/4; nearby errors contract. This is a local derivative comparison, not a required abstract fixed-point theorem.

parts.label: (c)
parts.question: Starting at 1.5, use the suitable iteration to find alpha to 4 decimal places. Verify the rounding with a sign-change bracket.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Iterate h without premature rounding to $1.557145599$. [A1] $f(1.55705)<0<f(1.55715)$. [A1] $\alpha=1.5571$ to 4 decimal places.

caie9709.fullSolution:
(a) [B1] $f(1)=-1$, $f(2)=\ln2>0$, and f is continuous. [B1] $f'=1+1/x>0$, hence the root is unique.

(b) [M1] Each fixed-point equation rearranges to $x+\ln x=2$. [A1] $g'(\alpha)=-\alpha$, so its magnitude exceeds 1; it is locally unstable. [A1] $h'(x)=(1-1/x)/2$, so on $[1,2]$ it is between 0 and 1/4; nearby errors contract. This is a local derivative comparison, not a required abstract fixed-point theorem.

(c) [M1] Iterate h without premature rounding to $1.557145599$. [A1] $f(1.55705)<0<f(1.55715)$. [A1] $\alpha=1.5571$ to 4 decimal places.

caie9709.context: Points A and B are $(1,2,-1)$ and $(3,-2,1)$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Find the vector AB and an equation of the line through A and B.
parts.solutionOutline: [B1] $\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,-4,2)$. [A1] $\mathbf r=(1,2,-1)+t(2,-4,2)$, $t\in\mathbb R$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Find the point on this line whose x-coordinate is 5.

parts.label: (a)
parts.question: Show that the lines intersect and find the intersection.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Equate x and y: $1+2\lambda=3+\mu$, $-\lambda=-4+\mu$. [A1] $\lambda=2$, $\mu=2$. [B1] Both give z=4, verifying the third coordinate. [A1] Intersection $(5,-2,4)$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.question: Find the acute angle between the lines, giving an exact expression.
parts.solutionOutline: [M1] Use direction vectors a=(2,-1,1), b=(1,1,0); $a\cdot b=1$. [M1] $|a|=\sqrt6$, $|b|=\sqrt2$. [A1] $\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/(2\sqrt3))$. No plane or vector product is needed.
